[9] I am also not persuaded that the RPD erred in assessing the risk posed to the Appellants by Knights Templar,11 described as a splinter group or successor of LFM.12 The Appellants themselves advanced the submission before the RPD that Knights Templar was the same continuous organization.13 After noting LFM's reported presence in Guerrero and Mexico City, and the fact that the organization was largely driven out of Michoácan by Knights Templar, the RPD then assessed whether Knights Templar had a presence in Yucatán and noted nothing in the NDP suggested as much.14 This does not mean that the panel misunderstood the claim, but rather, that it was being thorough by considering the reach of the successor organization.

[10] While the Appellants argue on appeal that LFM has a national reach, including a presence in Yucatán, they have not actually cited any evidence to establish this.15 The documentation before me supports the RPD's findings. LFM was once influential in Michoácan and surrounding states, but was largely driven out of Michoácan by Knights Templar.16 Remaining LFM fragments are reported to have been active in Guerrero and Mexico states, including working-class suburbs of Mexico City.17 A group calling itself La Nueva Familia Michoacana has been reportedly active in parts of Guerrero and Michoacán.18 Before the RPD, the Appellants also submitted that LFM was sometimes aligned with the Cartel Jalisco New Generation ("CJNG"), which has a presence in Campache and Quintana Roo.19 However, the Appellants have not cited any evidence indicating these groups are operating in Yucatán.

[11] The Appellants have not made any submissions about Los Pelones on appeal, but their narrative indicated that they feared this group as well; the man who killed the Principal Appellant's father in 2001 later went on to join this group, and, according to their allegations, the group was active in their hometown in Guerrero.20 However, they have not indicated that they were personally targeted by Los Pelones. Counsel before the RPD submitted that the group had a presence in Quintana Roo.21 However, the Appellants have not cited any evidence to suggest the group is present in Yucatán, and the NDP documentation does not indicate this is the case.22

[13] As the RPD explained in its decision, the Appellants and others in their small village were targeted by LFM, who wanted their land.24 According to the Principal Appellant's evidence, he and his family were threatened with death if they did not leave their town and the state of Guerrero.25 They subsequently fled and came to Canada. The real issue is why the agents of persecution would remain motivated to pursue the Appellants upon return, given, as the RPD noted, the family complied with their demands. The Appellants have not actually addressed this issue on appeal; their counsel's submissions on the first prong are largely focused on the ability of cartels to track people.26

[14] Without further evidence or submissions to establish an ongoing motivation on the part of the agents of persecution, I agree with the RPD that the Appellants have failed to establish that they face a personal risk to life, torture, or cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in the proposed IFA.
Appellants have not established relocation would be unreasonable in their circumstances

[15] The Appellants also submit that the panel failed to consider the particular circumstances of the Associate and Minor Appellants when concluding the family could relocate to Mérida.27 Again, a review of the hearing shows that neither the Appellants nor their counsel raised specific considerations for the Associate and Minor Appellants before the RPD.28

[16] While counsel before the RPD referenced "entrenched gender discrimination" in his oral submissions,29 he failed to explain how it related to the Associate Appellant's ability to relocate. I note that the Associate Appellant did not work outside of the home in Mexico,30 and the Appellants have not argued that gender discrimination would prevent her from working upon return. In the absence of more specific submissions, the Appellants have not established that gender discrimination makes the proposed IFA unreasonable. With respect to the children, counsel before the RPD referenced "age" generally in relation to all of the claimants,31 and also mentioned the size of the family, which he submitted would make it difficult for the Principal Appellant to provide sufficient financial support.32 No further submissions were provided. The RPD concluded the Principal Appellant could pursue work in the construction industry, if not farming, in Mérida.33 The Appellants have not challenged this finding on appeal.

[17] Considering this, I do not find that the RPD erred by failing to assess more specific factors for the Associate and Minor Appellants. Moreover, despite arguing that the panel erred in its analysis with respect to the Associate and Minor Appellants, counsel has not actually indicated why it would be unreasonable for them to relocate on appeal, nor has any documentation been cited in support of this submission.34 In light of this, the Appellants have not established, on a balance of probabilities, that relocation would be unreasonable in the Associate and Minor Appellants' circumstances.

[19] However, having reviewed the recording of the hearing, including counsel's oral submissions, I note that neither the Appellants nor their counsel actually advanced any arguments about the pandemic before the RPD. The documents they submitted into evidence were primarily focused on cartel violence and were dealt with by the RPD in its reasons.37 For these reasons, I do not find the panel erred in failing to address the issue in further depth.

[20] The Appellants further submit on appeal that rising cartel violence and diverted state resources would render relocation unreasonable in the wake of the pandemic.38 A review of the documents on Covid-19 submitted by the Appellants before the RPD shows several articles about increased cartel-related violence and fewer state resources to combat crime, along with tallies of Mexico's Covid-19 case counts.39 However, none of this evidence specifically relates to the proposed IFA of Mérida or the state of Yucatán, which has been ranked the safest state in Mexico.40 On a balance of probabilities, I am unable to conclude that criminal activity in the wake of the pandemic renders the proposed IFA unreasonable.

[21] The Appellants also cite evidence indicating that Mexico has the third highest fatality rate from the pandemic globally, after the United States and Brazil.41 They highlight evidence indicating that 15.5 per cent of the Mexican population does not have access to healthcare; as a result, they argue they most likely would not be able to access healthcare if they contract Covid-19.42 While a minority of Mexicans continue to lack access to healthcare, the majority of the population does have access, and this rate is improving. The full passage relied on by counsel indicates that the rate of those lacking access to healthcare has fallen from 21.5 to 15.5 per cent between 2012 and 2016.43 Based on this information, I am unable to conclude, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellants would lack access to medical care if required upon return.

[22] Finally, I am not persuaded by counsel's submission that the Appellants would have to cut ties with relatives in their hometown, which would render the proposed IFA unreasonable.44 The Appellants have failed to establish an ongoing motivation on the part of the agents of persecution to harm them. Communication with relatives would therefore not put them at risk.

[23] Relocation will always involve some level of hardship. The threshold to find an IFA objectively unreasonable is very high and requires, at a minimum, concrete evidence of adverse conditions which would jeopardize the Appellants' life and safety.45 The Appellants bear the onus of establishing that it is unreasonable to expect them to seek safety in a different part of the country. In this case, they have failed to do so. The RPD did not err in its conclusion on the second prong.

In this case, they have failed to do so. The RPD did not err in its conclusion on the second prong.

REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW

[1] These are my reasons for dismissing the appeal of XXXX XXXX XXXX ("Principal Appellant"), Concepcion XXXX XXXX XXXX ("Associate Appellant"), and their children XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX ("Minor Appellants").

[2] The Appellants are citizens of Mexico. They fear the La Familia Michoacana ("LFM") and Los Pelones cartels. The Refugee Protection Division ("RPD") accepted the family's allegations as credible, but determined they had a viable internal flight alternative ("IFA") in Mérida, Yucatán.

[3] On appeal, the Appellants challenge this finding. They also argue that the RPD's decision should be overturned because the panel failed to independently assess the risk facing the Associate and Minor Appellants.
SCOPE OF THE APPEAL

[4] Generally, I must review a decision of the RPD on a standard of correctness.1 The exception to this rule is where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in assessing the credibility of oral testimony, which may attract deference in particular cases.2 In this case, however, the RPD had no advantage. I have therefore considered whether its decision was correct.
[5] The Appellants have not presented any new evidence on appeal. They have requested an oral hearing; however, in the absence of any new evidence, I have no jurisdiction to convene one.3
ANALYSIS

[6] The determinative issue on appeal remains the existence of a viable IFA for the Appellants in Mérida. For the following reasons, I am not persuaded by the Appellants' submissions and find that the RPD did not err in determining the family could safely relocate.

[7] The test for IFA is two-pronged. The Board must be satisfied on a balance of probabilities that there is no serious possibility of persecution or personal risk to life, torture, or cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in the proposed location,4 and conditions in the IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable, in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claimant, for them to seek refuge there.5 Both prongs of the test must be satisfied for a viable IFA to be established. Once the issue is raised, the onus is on the claimant to demonstrate that they do not have a viable IFA.
Panel did not err in failing to assess risk not advanced by Appellants

[8] First, while I agree with the Appellants that the RPD did not specifically analyze threats to the Associate and Minor Appellants,6 the Appellants did not actually raise any threats independent of the Principal Appellant's narrative and testimony. While the Basis of Claim narrative references a fear of sexual violence for the female Appellants, this was based on the same set of facts as the Principal Appellant's claim.7 A narrative was only submitted for the Principal Appellant; the rest of the family relied on it.8 An associate in the office of counsel on appeal represented the Appellants before the RPD. A review of the hearing, including counsel's oral submissions, shows that no additional grounds of risk were advanced.9 The RPD therefore did not err by failing to do a separate analysis as alleged.10
Panel did not err in assessing risk posed by related cartel

[9] I am also not persuaded that the RPD erred in assessing the risk posed to the Appellants by Knights Templar,11 described as a splinter group or successor of LFM.12 The Appellants themselves advanced the submission before the RPD that Knights Templar was the same continuous organization.13 After noting LFM's reported presence in Guerrero and Mexico City, and the fact that the organization was largely driven out of Michoácan by Knights Templar, the RPD then assessed whether Knights Templar had a presence in Yucatán and noted nothing in the NDP suggested as much.14 This does not mean that the panel misunderstood the claim, but rather, that it was being thorough by considering the reach of the successor organization.

[10] While the Appellants argue on appeal that LFM has a national reach, including a presence in Yucatán, they have not actually cited any evidence to establish this.15 The documentation before me supports the RPD's findings. LFM was once influential in Michoácan and surrounding states, but was largely driven out of Michoácan by Knights Templar.16 Remaining LFM fragments are reported to have been active in Guerrero and Mexico states, including working-class suburbs of Mexico City.17 A group calling itself La Nueva Familia Michoacana has been reportedly active in parts of Guerrero and Michoacán.18 Before the RPD, the Appellants also submitted that LFM was sometimes aligned with the Cartel Jalisco New Generation ("CJNG"), which has a presence in Campache and Quintana Roo.19 However, the Appellants have not cited any evidence indicating these groups are operating in Yucatán.

[11] The Appellants have not made any submissions about Los Pelones on appeal, but their narrative indicated that they feared this group as well; the man who killed the Principal Appellant's father in 2001 later went on to join this group, and, according to their allegations, the group was active in their hometown in Guerrero.20 However, they have not indicated that they were personally targeted by Los Pelones. Counsel before the RPD submitted that the group had a presence in Quintana Roo.21 However, the Appellants have not cited any evidence to suggest the group is present in Yucatán, and the NDP documentation does not indicate this is the case.22
Appellants have not established ongoing motivation of agents of persecution

[12] In any event, I find the determinative issue on the first prong is a lack of motivation on the part of the agents of persecution. I agree with the Appellants' submission that, when motivated to do so, cartels have the means to locate individuals throughout the country.23 However, in my independent assessment, the Appellants have failed to demonstrate that their agents of persecution have an ongoing motivation to harm them.

[13] As the RPD explained in its decision, the Appellants and others in their small village were targeted by LFM, who wanted their land.24 According to the Principal Appellant's evidence, he and his family were threatened with death if they did not leave their town and the state of Guerrero.25 They subsequently fled and came to Canada. The real issue is why the agents of persecution would remain motivated to pursue the Appellants upon return, given, as the RPD noted, the family complied with their demands. The Appellants have not actually addressed this issue on appeal; their counsel's submissions on the first prong are largely focused on the ability of cartels to track people.26

[14] Without further evidence or submissions to establish an ongoing motivation on the part of the agents of persecution, I agree with the RPD that the Appellants have failed to establish that they face a personal risk to life, torture, or cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in the proposed IFA.
Appellants have not established relocation would be unreasonable in their circumstances

[15] The Appellants also submit that the panel failed to consider the particular circumstances of the Associate and Minor Appellants when concluding the family could relocate to Mérida.27 Again, a review of the hearing shows that neither the Appellants nor their counsel raised specific considerations for the Associate and Minor Appellants before the RPD.28

[16] While counsel before the RPD referenced "entrenched gender discrimination" in his oral submissions,29 he failed to explain how it related to the Associate Appellant's ability to relocate. I note that the Associate Appellant did not work outside of the home in Mexico,30 and the Appellants have not argued that gender discrimination would prevent her from working upon return. In the absence of more specific submissions, the Appellants have not established that gender discrimination makes the proposed IFA unreasonable. With respect to the children, counsel before the RPD referenced "age" generally in relation to all of the claimants,31 and also mentioned the size of the family, which he submitted would make it difficult for the Principal Appellant to provide sufficient financial support.32 No further submissions were provided. The RPD concluded the Principal Appellant could pursue work in the construction industry, if not farming, in Mérida.33 The Appellants have not challenged this finding on appeal.

[17] Considering this, I do not find that the RPD erred by failing to assess more specific factors for the Associate and Minor Appellants. Moreover, despite arguing that the panel erred in its analysis with respect to the Associate and Minor Appellants, counsel has not actually indicated why it would be unreasonable for them to relocate on appeal, nor has any documentation been cited in support of this submission.34 In light of this, the Appellants have not established, on a balance of probabilities, that relocation would be unreasonable in the Associate and Minor Appellants' circumstances.

[18] While not raised in submissions before the RPD, the Appellants provided documentation on the impact of Covid-19 on relocation, and the panel addressed this issue in its reasons.35 It found that the pandemic had affected Mexicans generally, and that the Appellants had failed to put forward specific submissions as to how it would affect them on return. It noted, for instance, that there was no evidence of pre-existing medical conditions. On appeal, the Appellants argue that the panel erred by importing a generalized risk analysis into the second prong of the IFA and by failing to consider counsel's submissions and the Appellants' testimony on Covid-19, specifically its impact on access to employment, housing, healthcare, and food.36

[19] However, having reviewed the recording of the hearing, including counsel's oral submissions, I note that neither the Appellants nor their counsel actually advanced any arguments about the pandemic before the RPD. The documents they submitted into evidence were primarily focused on cartel violence and were dealt with by the RPD in its reasons.37 For these reasons, I do not find the panel erred in failing to address the issue in further depth.

[20] The Appellants further submit on appeal that rising cartel violence and diverted state resources would render relocation unreasonable in the wake of the pandemic.38 A review of the documents on Covid-19 submitted by the Appellants before the RPD shows several articles about increased cartel-related violence and fewer state resources to combat crime, along with tallies of Mexico's Covid-19 case counts.39 However, none of this evidence specifically relates to the proposed IFA of Mérida or the state of Yucatán, which has been ranked the safest state in Mexico.40 On a balance of probabilities, I am unable to conclude that criminal activity in the wake of the pandemic renders the proposed IFA unreasonable.

[21] The Appellants also cite evidence indicating that Mexico has the third highest fatality rate from the pandemic globally, after the United States and Brazil.41 They highlight evidence indicating that 15.5 per cent of the Mexican population does not have access to healthcare; as a result, they argue they most likely would not be able to access healthcare if they contract Covid-19.42 While a minority of Mexicans continue to lack access to healthcare, the majority of the population does have access, and this rate is improving. The full passage relied on by counsel indicates that the rate of those lacking access to healthcare has fallen from 21.5 to 15.5 per cent between 2012 and 2016.43 Based on this information, I am unable to conclude, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellants would lack access to medical care if required upon return.

[22] Finally, I am not persuaded by counsel's submission that the Appellants would have to cut ties with relatives in their hometown, which would render the proposed IFA unreasonable.44 The Appellants have failed to establish an ongoing motivation on the part of the agents of persecution to harm them. Communication with relatives would therefore not put them at risk.

[23] Relocation will always involve some level of hardship. The threshold to find an IFA objectively unreasonable is very high and requires, at a minimum, concrete evidence of adverse conditions which would jeopardize the Appellants' life and safety.45 The Appellants bear the onus of establishing that it is unreasonable to expect them to seek safety in a different part of the country. In this case, they have failed to do so. The RPD did not err in its conclusion on the second prong.
CONCLUSION

[24] For the reasons set out above, I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
